# kiss-ssg

> A small, dependency-driven static site generator for Node. MVC-style: Handlebars views, JSON/HTTP/function models, JS controllers. ESM package (Node ≥22.12); engine in `lib/`, entry `lib/kiss.js`. No build step, no bundler.

Install: `npm install kiss-ssg --save-dev`. `import Kiss from 'kiss-ssg'` (CJS `require('kiss-ssg')` also works on Node ≥22.12). Everything is driven by a `Kiss` instance built with `new Kiss(config)` and used via a chainable API. Pages are queued (not rendered) by `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.scan()`; `.generate()` renders and writes them; `.sitemap()`/`.watch()` are opt-in extras. `config` and its resolved values are available in every view as `this.config`.

## API

- `.page(options)` — register one page. `options.view` (required): a `.hbs` filename relative to `config.folders.pages`, or a template string. `options.model`: a `.json` filename (relative to `config.folders.models`), an `http(s)://` URL (headers, timeout, retries and an on-disk cache come from `config.fetch`, below; a response with a non-2xx status fails that page — an error body is never used as the model, nor cached), a plain object, or a folder name (loads every `*.json` in it as an array). `options.controller`: a function `({model}) => optionsPatch`, or a `.js` filename relative to `config.folders.controllers`, run after the model resolves — commonly used to reshape/sort the model or derive `slug`. Controllers should stay pure: return new values rather than mutating `options.model` (or a nested object such as `options.config.folders`) in place. How much an in-place mutation costs you depends on the model kind — a `.json` file, a models folder, or an `http(s)://` URL model is re-resolved on every build and on every `.watch()` whole-site rebuild, so an in-place mutation of one of those is contained to that single build. A **plain object** model is different: it is replayed from a shallow snapshot of the original `.page()` call, so an object model (or a closed-over value) a controller mutated in place is still mutated on the next rebuild — an in-place `push`/assignment accumulates one more change per save, and the dev server drifts further from what a fresh build would produce with every edit. Returning new values sidesteps the distinction entirely. A controller that throws, a filename that does not exist, or a file that does not export a function fails that page and makes `complete()` reject. `options.title`, `options.description`, `options.path`, `options.slug`, `options.ext` (default `html`; a leading `.` is stripped and the rest slugified, so an `ext` derived from model data cannot steer the output path — `'.xml'` → `xml`, `'../x'` → `x`). `options.generate` (default `true`): set `false` to skip building this one page entirely — nothing is written, and it claims no output path, so it cannot collide with a page that is. `.generate()`/`.complete()` still resolve normally — the way to conditionally drop a page, e.g. a `.pages()` fan-out item that fails a check in its controller. `options.id`: this page's identity — what `{{link "<id>"}}` resolves (see `## Helpers`). It defaults to the view's route without its extension (`blog/listing.hbs` → `blog/listing`), so most pages need nothing; set it when you want a stable name (`id: 'blog'`) or when two `.page()` calls render one view (pagination), where **neither** gets the default id and a `notice` says so. On a `.pages()` fan-out an item's default id is the registration's route — or the registration's own `id`, used as a **prefix** — plus the item's slug (`blog/post/the-cascara-experiment`), and a *record* may carry its own `id`, which wins outright; the registration's `id` is never broadcast to the items, the same rule `aliases` follows. A controller may return one. Two pages claiming one explicit id fail the build (`Page id already claimed: <id>`), an explicit id beats a colliding default one, and a `generate: false` page claims no id at all. ``options.aliases`: old URL paths this page now answers (`aliases: ['/old-slug', '/news/2024/thing.html']`), each written as one `301` line of `<build>/_redirects` — see `## Checking a build`; on a `.pages()` fan-out the aliases belong to each **record**, never to the registration, so one item's `aliases` cannot be broadcast over the whole fan-out. `options.config`: per-page config overrides, merged over the global `config` for that page only. Every page renders with its own shallow copy of the resolved config, so a controller mutating `options.config` changes that page alone — not the other pages, the instance's `config`, or the sitemap (nested objects such as `folders` are shared, and the engine never mutates them). `slug`/`path` are inferred from `view`'s file path if omitted — but only when `view` is a `.hbs` filename; a template string gets a random `snippet-N` slug and no path, since its own markup is not a file path. Slugs (and each `path` segment) are normalised by `utils.toSlug`: accented Latin is transliterated (`'Über uns'` → `uber-uns`), everything else outside `a-z0-9` becomes `-`, leading/trailing dashes are trimmed, and a title in a script with no Latin mapping (CJK, Hangul, Cyrillic) falls back to a short stable hash (`p-9736ca69`) so such pages stay distinct instead of all claiming one file. Two pages that resolve to the same output path **fail the build** (`complete()` rejects, naming the path) — only one of them would ever exist on disk.
- `.pages(options)` — same as `.page()`, but `options.model` must resolve to an array (or a models folder), and it fans out one page per item, appending `-N` to the slug per item unless the controller sets an explicit `slug`. A bad item fails only its own page: if the controller throws for one item the rest of the fan-out is still registered and built, and every bad item is reported separately by `complete()` as `<view> [item N: <slug>]` (no output path exists to name it by).
- `.scan()` — auto-discovers every `.hbs` under `config.folders.pages` you have not already registered (by `view`, so a `.page()` earlier in the same chain wins and the view is not built twice), and calls `.page()` on each with default options. The simplest way to build a whole site: `kiss.scan().generate()`. Under `.watch()` the scan is repeated on every whole-site rebuild, so page files you add or delete while the dev server runs are picked up.
- `.generate(callback)` — waits for every queued page's model to resolve, then renders and writes each page exactly once (in a normal build HTML is minified via `html-minifier-terser`, comments included; under `dev: true` minification is skipped altogether, so dev output keeps its comments and whitespace and a dev build never loads the minifier). `callback(data)` fires after every page has been attempted — including any that failed to render or write; page failures don't surface here, they surface via `complete()`. `data` is `[{ id, data }]`, one entry per queued promise **in registration order** — the automatic construction-time asset copy is queued first, so `data[0]` is that copy's result (`{ id, data: 'Copied assets: …' }`), not your first page. Use `getModelByID(id, data)` (below) rather than indexing by position. An error thrown by the callback itself (or a rejection from a promise it returns) is a build failure of its own, recorded as `<generate callback>` and reported by `complete()`. Chainable — returns the `Kiss` instance. To await the whole build use `await kiss.complete()`.
- `.complete(callback)` — resolves after every queued page and any `sitemap()` call has finished writing; resolves with the same `data` array `generate` receives. "Every queued page" includes pages queued from a `generate` callback, whether the callback queues them synchronously or after an `await` (the promise an `async` callback returns is part of what `complete()` waits for), and it includes any page queued after the last `generate()` call: `complete()` renders whatever no `generate()` pass reached, so a page whose model resolved late — or one a callback's `scan()` discovered — is never silently dropped from a build that reports success. It renders nothing if you never called `generate()` at all. Work a _synchronous_ callback defers to a later tick (a `setTimeout`-ed `.page()`) is still outside the build — queue pages synchronously, or from an `async` callback. Rejects with an `AggregateError` — `err.failures` = `[{ view, buildTo, error }]`, message `"N page(s) failed to build: <buildTo paths>"` (build paths, not views, since `.pages()` fan-out gives failed entries the same view; entries with no output path, such as a failing controller or callback, are named by `view` instead) — if any page failed to render or write, any controller failed, or a `generate`/`sitemap` callback threw; other pages still build, and the `generate` callback still fires. In `dev: true` a dev server that cannot bind `config.port` is a build failure too, reported as `<dev server>`. It rejects **once per build**: a second `complete()` in the same build resolves instead of rejecting again, so the pattern of calling `complete()` from inside a `generate` callback cannot leave a second, unhandled rejection behind. A failed build never runs `complete()`'s own callback. A model failure is not a build failure: it is logged and skipped, and shows up in the resolved data as `{ id, data: null, error }`. A `.hbs` view whose file cannot be read (missing or misspelled) **is** a build failure: that page fails and `complete()` rejects, rather than the filename being written into the output.
- `.report()` — the last settled build as data, or `null` before the first `.complete()` has settled (a watch rebuild replaces it with its own). `{ ok, mode, buildDir, duration, pages, failures, assets, sitemap, pipeline, llms, aikb, links, redirects, feed }`: `ok` is "nothing failed"; `mode` is `'build'`, or `'check'` when the build was staged and thrown away (see `## Checking a build`); `buildDir` is the folder you asked for, never the staging sibling a `'atomic'` build writes to; `duration` is ms from `new Kiss()`; `pages` is `{ view, buildTo, ok, hash, id }` per queued page, in registration order (an inline template's `view` is elided to its first line; `hash` is the sha1 of the bytes that page wrote, or `null` when it wrote none — a page that failed, or one with `generate: false`; `id` is the page's identity, what `{{link}}` resolves, and is `null` for an inline template, a `generate: false` page and a default id two pages arrived at); `failures` is `{ view, buildTo, message }` — the same list `err.failures` carries, with the `Error` reduced to its message so the whole thing survives `JSON.stringify`; `assets` is `{ source, target }` per emitted file (the path a template asks for, and the file that is actually there under `config.assets`); `sitemap` is the `sitemap.xml` this build wrote, or `null`; `pipeline` is `{ name, ok, duration }` per `config.assets.pipeline` step, in order, and `[]` when there are none; `llms` is the `llms.txt` this build wrote, or `null`; `aikb` is `null` unless the site has a knowledge base to report on (`config.folders.aikb` set, and a record already made — see `## Checking a build`), and otherwise `{ folder, written, notes: { missing, dead, stale, dangling }, subjects }` — where that knowledge base lives, whether this build wrote it (`true` only for a passing `npx kiss-ssg aikb` run; every ordinary build reports `false`), the four note findings (paths, except `dangling`'s `<note path>: <token>`), and `{ kind, id, note, hash }` per subject of *this* build, which is where the hash to stamp a note with comes from before a record has been made. The same object is on the rejection as `err.report`, so a failed build is readable as data without catching and re-deriving anything. `links`, `redirects` and `feed` are **new in this version**, appended in that order after `aikb`, and each is `null` until the build in question did that piece of work — which is not the same as "it did it and found nothing". `links` carries the broken-internal-link scan of this build's own output as `{ checked, broken: [{ page, href }] }` (`null` on a dev build, on a watch rebuild and under `config.links.check: false`); `redirects` carries what the build did about page `aliases` as `{ file, aliases, removed, collisions, moved }` — the `_redirects` it wrote, how many alias paths went into it, the pages the last record had that this build no longer has and no alias covers, the aliases a live page already answers, and `{ id, from, to }` per page the record and this build share an `id` with whose path changed and whose old path no alias covers; `feed` is the feed file this build wrote, like `sitemap` and `llms`. Every path in the three is named against the build folder you asked for, never the staging sibling. It is additive: `complete()` still resolves with the `data` array and still rejects with the `AggregateError`.
- `.sitemap(options, callback)` — writes `sitemap.xml` to `config.folders.build`, derived from every registered page. Requires `config.siteUrl` (logs an error and skips, does not throw, if unset). Can be called before or after `.generate()` — both just wait on the same internal promise queue. Per-page opt-out: `ignoreSitemap: true` in that page's `.page()`/`.pages()` options; a `generate: false` page is left out too. Per-page overrides: `sitemapPriority` (default `'1.00'`), `sitemapChangefreq` (omitted from the XML unless set), `sitemapLastmod` (default: one timestamp shared by all pages, captured when `.sitemap()` runs). `options.overwrite` (default `true`) — set `false` to skip (re)writing if `sitemap.xml` already exists; only has an effect if `cleanBuild: false` too, since the default `cleanBuild: true` already empties the whole build dir — including any prior `sitemap.xml` — before `.sitemap()` ever runs.
- `.llms(options, callback)` — writes `llms.txt` to `config.folders.build`: the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) index an answer engine reads first, derived from the same registry the sitemap is. Same lifecycle as `.sitemap()` — chainable, callable before or after `.generate()`, waiting on the same internal queue, and re-run by every whole-site `watch` rebuild. `options.title` (required) is the file's `# ` heading; `options.summary` (required) is the `> ` blockquote, and is either the text itself or a path (relative to `process.cwd()`) to a `.md`/`.txt` file holding it; `options.notes` (optional, same text-or-file rule) becomes a trailing `## Notes` section; `options.sections` maps a top-level path segment to a heading (`{ courses: 'Courses' }`, the key `root` naming the section that holds pages with no path, default `Pages`), and an unmapped segment is title-cased; `options.overwrite` (default `true`) behaves exactly as the sitemap's. A missing `config.siteUrl`, `title` or `summary` logs an error and skips the file — it never throws, and the callback does not fire. Pages are grouped by the first segment of their `path` (root pages first) and listed in registration order as `- [title](url): description`, with the description omitted when the page has none and the title falling back to the page's slug, title-cased. Each URL is the **same string** the page's own `{{canonical}}` and its `<loc>` in `sitemap.xml` are, built by the same code. Per-page: `ignoreLlms: true` keeps a page out; `ignoreSitemap: true` and `generate: false` keep it out automatically; `llmsSection: 'Name'` overrides the group it lands in. `callback(text)` receives the rendered file.
- `.feed(options, callback)` — writes an RSS 2.0 feed to `config.folders.build`: the third file derived from the same registry as `sitemap.xml` and `llms.txt`, so an item can never name a URL the site does not serve. Same lifecycle as `.sitemap()` and `.llms()` — chainable, callable before or after `.generate()`, waiting on the same internal queue, and re-run by every whole-site `watch` rebuild. `options.title` (required) is the channel's `<title>`; `options.description` is its `<description>`; `options.section` limits the feed to one top-level `path` segment (`{ section: 'blog' }` — omit it for every page); `options.limit` (default `20`) caps the items; `options.filename` (default `feed.xml`) names the file inside the build folder; `options.dateField` (default `'date'`) names the field each item's date comes from; `options.overwrite` (default `true`) behaves exactly as the sitemap's. A missing `config.siteUrl` or `title` logs an error and skips the file — it never throws, and the callback does not fire. **One item per page that carries a date**, newest first (the URL breaks a tie), where the date is `options[dateField] ?? options.model[dateField]` — so a post can be dated in its `.page()`/`.pages()` options or in its model, and either way it is the same field. A `Date`, epoch milliseconds, or any string `new Date()` parses is accepted; a value that cannot be read logs one warning and the page is treated as undated. Pages with no date are simply left out, silently — most of a site is undated. Per-page: `ignoreFeed: true` keeps a page out; `ignoreSitemap: true` and `generate: false` keep it out automatically. Each `<link>`/`<guid>` is the **same string** as the page's own `{{canonical}}` and its `<loc>` in `sitemap.xml`; `<title>` and `<description>` are derived exactly as `llms.txt` derives them. `<lastBuildDate>` is the newest item's date rather than the wall clock, so two identical builds produce byte-identical files. `report().feed` names the file written (against the build folder you asked for, never a staging sibling), or `null`. `callback(text)` receives the rendered document.
- `.watch(options)` — starts a `chokidar` watcher on `config.folders.src` (only meaningful with `dev: true`, which also starts a livereload dev server on `config.port`, default `3001`, bound to `config.devHost`, with live reload on `config.livereloadPort`); rebuilds just the affected page(s), or the whole site if a changed file can't be matched to a queued page. Editing a partial or a layout re-registers the partials and re-renders **only the pages that rendered it** — learned at render time, so a partial chosen with `lookup`, reached through another partial, or used as a layout all count — without re-resolving any model (URL models included) or re-running any controller; a partial no page has rendered yet re-renders every page and logs a notice naming it. With `verbose: true` a dev build also writes `dependency-graph.json` (`{ partial: [built pages…] }`) beside `debug.json`, and each page's `.json` sibling lists the `partials` it used. Every other non-page change is a whole-site rebuild. A whole-site rebuild replays every `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.scan()` registration from scratch, so edited models and controllers take effect (controller files are reloaded from disk, ESM and CommonJS alike) — which means every URL model is fetched again on every rebuild unless you set `config.fetch.cache`; a single-page rebuild is a template re-render. A whole-site rebuild also deletes output files the previous build wrote that the new one no longer produces (a removed fan-out model, a changed slug, or a page `.scan()` had discovered whose `.hbs` file you deleted — a page you registered by name instead keeps failing the build until you remove the call) and re-runs `.sitemap()` if you ever called it. Creating a file under `src/` rebuilds the whole site too, so a partial or layout you add mid-session is registered and usable straight away (a file created empty is picked up once it has content — an event on an empty file is ignored, which is also what keeps a slow truncate-then-write save from rebuilding against a half-written file), and a new page `.hbs` is built as well if you used `.scan()` (a rebuild scans the pages folder again; on an explicitly registered site you still add the `.page()` call yourself). Deleting a partial or layout unregisters it, so any page still referencing it fails the rebuild with `The partial <name> could not be found` instead of quietly rendering the deleted content until you restart. `options.entry` (default `process.argv[1]`): the script whose change triggers a full rebuild. The browser is told to reload **once per rebuild, after every page has been written** (and once when the first build finishes), never once per file — so a reload can never land on a page the rebuild has not re-rendered yet. An edited stylesheet reloads that stylesheet alone, leaving the page's state alone.
- `.close()` — stops the file watcher and dev server (dev mode / after `.watch()`); returns a Promise that resolves once any in-flight rebuild has finished, so nothing is written after it.
- `.copyAssets(sourceDir, targetDir)` — compiles every `*.scss`/`*.sass` under `sourceDir` to a sibling `.css` and copies everything else straight through to `targetDir`. Runs automatically once at construction time for `config.folders.assets` → `config.folders.build`; callable again for extra asset directories. Calls run one after another in registration order, not concurrently. Every emitted file is recorded in the instance's asset manifest — that is what `{{asset}}` reads, and what `config.assets` renames (see `## Config`).
- `.registerPartials()` — re-registers every partial and layout from disk (`folders.partials`, `folders.layouts`, plus `.md`/`.html` partials), unregistering any name whose file has since gone; returns the list of registered names. **Every entry of `kiss.handlebars.partials` is a function** — a compiled template that also records which page invoked it, which is what scopes a watch-mode partial edit to the pages that used it. `handlebars-layouts` recompiles a string layout on every page render and never caches it, so compiling at registration is also what stops a layout being recompiled once per page. Code of yours that renders an entry by name must accept a function, and must pass its own `options.data` through: `const p = kiss.handlebars.partials[name]; typeof p === 'function' ? p(ctx, { data: options.data }) : kiss.handlebars.compile(p)(ctx, { data: options.data })` (it was a string only until the partial's first render anyway). That data frame is how the page is recorded as using the partial: a bare `p(ctx)` renders correctly, but under `.watch()` that page is not re-rendered when the partial changes (unless no page recorded it at all, when every page is). Runs automatically at construction and on every watch rebuild — call it yourself to pick up partials added or removed at runtime outside `.watch()`. A `.md` or `.html` partial is a Handlebars template like any other: the built-in and registered helpers run inside it (`{{asset "js/site.js"}}` in a `.html` partial resolves), and its `.md` body is rendered to HTML first.
- `.viewStats()` — logs the queued-promise and prepared-page counts, and (with `verbose: true`) writes `debug.json` — one entry per page, `{ view, buildTo, runCount, options }` — into `config.folders.build`. Chainable; use it from a `generate` callback to see what a build actually produced.
- `.getModelByID(id, data)` — looks an entry up by `id` in the `[{ id, data }]` array `generate`/`complete` hand back, and returns its `.data` (or `{ error }` if there is no such id). The `id` is the model filename or URL you passed; object models get a hash instead. Use it to pull one page's resolved model out of the build data.
- `kiss.handlebars` — this instance's own Handlebars environment (`Handlebars.create()`, created per `Kiss`, so helpers and partials never leak between instances, and helpers registered on the global `handlebars` module are not seen); register custom helpers on it directly. Built-in helpers (`markdown`, `sass`, `offset`, `stringify`, `lookup`, `isActive`, `canonical`, `absUrl`, `asset`, `link`, `env`) are documented in `## Helpers` below.
- `kiss.remarkable` — this instance's own Markdown renderer (used for `.md` partials and the `markdown` helper).
- `import { utils } from 'kiss-ssg'` — `toSlug`, `sanitizePath`, `toTitleCase`, `trimLines`, `trimPath`, `posixPath`, `globFiles(dir, pattern)`, `hashId`, `toURLKey`, `toAbsoluteUrl(siteUrl, path)`, `toCanonicalPath`, `servedPathFor(pageURL)`.

## Config

Passed to `new Kiss(config)`. Defaults:

```js
{
  dev: false,          // starts a livereload dev server + file watcher; skips minification
  verbose: false,
  cleanBuild: true,     // true | false | 'atomic' — see below; true empties config.folders.build in the constructor
  extensionLess: false, // true: non-index pages build to <path>/<slug>/index.html instead of <path>/<slug>.html
  siteUrl: undefined,   // required by .sitemap() and the canonical/absUrl helpers
  sass: { includePaths: [] },
  fetch: {              // policy for http(s) models (per instance, not per page)
    headers: {},        // sent with every URL-model request (auth, accept)
    timeout: 10000,     // ms; the request is aborted and the page fails
    retries: 0,         // extra attempts on a network error or a 5xx; a 4xx is never retried
    cache: false,       // or a directory: successful bodies are cached there, keyed by url + headers
  },
  assets: {             // policy for the files copyAssets emits; all off = today's build
    hash: false,        // true: every emitted .css/.js is renamed to carry a content hash
    version: null,      // a string: nothing is renamed, {{asset}} appends ?v=<string>
    pipeline: [],       // ordered { name?, run, watch?, cwd? } commands run before the asset copy
  },
  markdown: {           // Remarkable options for .md partials and the {{markdown}} helper
    html: true,         // render raw HTML in the source rather than escaping it
    xhtmlOut: true,     // close single tags XHTML-style (<br />)
    breaks: false,      // true: every newline inside a paragraph becomes a <br />
  },
  links: {              // the broken-internal-link scan, run on a settled non-dev build
    check: true,        // false: skip it; the finding is advisory either way
  },
  port: 3001,           // dev server port
  livereloadPort: 35729, // live reload port; also the port injected into the dev-mode reload <script>
  devHost: '127.0.0.1',  // interface the dev + live reload servers bind to
  folders: {
    src: './src',
    pages: './src/pages',
    build: './public',
    assets: './src/assets',
    layouts: './src/layouts',
    partials: './src/partials',
    models: './src/models',
    controllers: './src/controllers',
    aikb: './AIKB',   // where `kiss-ssg aikb` records the site's knowledge base; source-side, committed, and not derived from src
  },
}
```

`cleanBuild` decides what happens to `config.folders.build`. `true` (the default) empties it with `fs.emptyDirSync` **in the `Kiss` constructor** — before any model resolves and before any page renders — and nothing puts it back if the build then fails, so a failed re-run leaves the folder empty or half-built. `false` never cleans, and stale files from earlier builds stay. `'atomic'` builds into a staging sibling (`<build>.kiss-staging-<pid>-<random>`) and swaps the whole folder into place only when `complete()` resolves: until that moment the previous output is untouched, a build that fails (or that you never `complete()`) leaves it exactly as it was, and `close()` removes the staging folder. Pages, assets, `sitemap.xml` and `debug.json` all follow the staging folder, including a `.copyAssets()` you aimed explicitly at the build folder. The swap is two renames (the old folder is renamed aside, staging is renamed in, then the old one is deleted), so the previous output is never gone while a copy is in progress, and a build that is killed mid-flight leaves a `<build>.kiss-staging-…` / `.kiss-old-…` sibling that the next run removes with one notice. `'atomic'` is for one-shot builds: in `dev: true` it degrades to `true` (the dev server serves the build folder from the start) and logs one notice saying so, and only `complete()` promotes — a chain that ends at `.generate()` never swaps anything in. Any other value throws. **If `config.folders.build` points at published output** — an archive of per-version builds, say — use `'atomic'`, and validate the folder name before you construct: an empty string interpolated into the path resolves to the parent folder, and `true` would empty the whole archive at construction. kiss refuses one shape of that at construction whatever `cleanBuild` says: a `build` that is the source folder, contains it, or is a filesystem root (`'.'`, `'/'`) throws, since cleaning it would delete the site's own source.

**Building more than one site from one source tree**: kiss has no "versions" concept — it is one `Kiss` instance per `folders.build`. An archive of per-version outputs (per-intake handbooks, a menu rebuilt each season) needs only: one `Kiss` per output with `folders.build` as the discriminator (`build: './menus/' + season`); an arbitrary config key carried into views as the per-build variable (`new Kiss({ season, ... })` read as `{{config.season}}`); `folders.assets: null` plus an explicit `copyAssets(src, buildDir)` when each output must own its assets rather than share a folder kiss keeps re-copying from; and `cleanBuild: 'atomic'` so a re-run fixing one output can never destroy or half-build another already published. Validate the value before it reaches `folders.build` — an empty or malformed one resolves against the parent of every output already there. See **Cleaning the build folder** above and `examples/7-versioned-outputs.js`.

`fetch` is the policy for `http(s)` models. `headers` goes out with every URL-model request — an `Authorization` header for an API that needs one, an `Accept` header for an API that offers several shapes. `timeout` (ms) aborts a request that never answers and fails that page rather than hanging the build; it is the one default with teeth, since before it existed a silent upstream stalled a build for ever. `retries` adds attempts after a network error or a 5xx, with a short linear backoff — a 4xx is never retried, because the server has already told you the request itself is wrong, and the rejection names how many attempts were made. `cache` is `false` or a directory path: a successful body is written there under a hash of the URL **and** the header set (a different token is a different entry), and every later resolution of that URL — later in this build, in the next `.watch()` rebuild, or in tomorrow's build in a new process — reads the file instead of fetching. A cached model is a build input, exactly like a `.json` file in `folders.models`: it makes `dev` mode and watch rebuilds stop paying a network round trip per remote model, and it lets an offline build work. There is no TTL — delete the directory (or one file in it) to refetch — and it is build output, so add it to `.gitignore`. An error response is never cached: the non-2xx guard stays authoritative over the cache. The block is merged one level deep, like `sass`, and applies per `Kiss` instance — there is no per-page override.

`assets` is the cache-busting policy for the files `.copyAssets()` emits, and it is read by the `{{asset}}` helper (below). With both keys at their defaults a build emits exactly the files and paths it always did. `hash: true` renames every emitted `.css` and `.js` to carry an 8-character hash of its **emitted** bytes (`css/site.css` → `css/site.a1b2c3d4.css`, and a `.scss` is hashed after sass compiled it), so a changed file is a new URL a cache has never seen and an unchanged one keeps its URL; the old file is deleted as the new one is written, so a watch-mode edit leaves one stylesheet in the build, not one per save. Nothing else is renamed — an image, a font or `robots.txt` is reached by URLs kiss does not rewrite (the ones inside a stylesheet, the ones a host asks for by a fixed name) — but every copied file is in the manifest, so `{{asset}}` resolves them all. `version: '1.4.5'` is the alternative: no file is renamed and `{{asset}}` appends `?v=1.4.5` instead, which suits a host that would rather not see new filenames. Setting both is a misconfiguration — the hashed filename wins and a warning says so. The block is merged one level deep, like `sass` and `fetch`, and applies per `Kiss` instance: the files are emitted once, so there is no per-page override.

`assets.pipeline` is how a site runs an external tool as part of the build — a CSS toolchain, an icon sprite, anything with a command line. Each step is `{ name?, run, watch?, cwd? }`. Every `run` is executed through a shell, in order, awaited, **before** the asset copy, so a tool that writes into the assets folder (`src/assets/css/site.css`) has its output copied into the build like any other asset — and again before the copy on every whole-site `watch` rebuild. A step that exits non-zero (or cannot be spawned) is a build failure like a failed page: `complete()` rejects, the failure is named `<pipeline: <name>>` in `err.failures`, and the pages and the asset copy still run so the whole build is still reported. `name` defaults to the first word of `run`; `cwd` defaults to `process.cwd()`; each command inherits `process.env` plus `KISS_BUILD`, `KISS_ASSETS` and `KISS_DEV` (`'1'`/`'0'`). `watch` is the dev-mode half: in `dev: true` only, it is started once after that step's `run` succeeded, kept for the session with its output going through the logger, and ended by `close()` — it is not started again by a rebuild, and a watch process that dies on its own is logged, not a build failure. Tailwind, end to end:

```js
assets: {
  pipeline: [
    {
      name: 'tailwind',
      run: 'npx @tailwindcss/cli -i src/styles/site.css -o src/assets/css/site.css --minify',
      watch: 'npx @tailwindcss/cli -i src/styles/site.css -o src/assets/css/site.css --minify --watch=always',
    },
  ],
}
```

`kiss-ssg check` runs the pipeline exactly as a build does, so a check is not read-only over your working tree: it regenerates whatever the steps generate (their output is a source file, which is why there is nothing extra for the check to discard). Scoped re-renders — a page view, a partial or a layout edit under `watch` — deliberately do **not** re-run the steps; a tool that must see those edits is what `watch` is for. A watch command gets no stdin from kiss, so a tool that stops when stdin closes needs its keep-alive flag — Tailwind's is `--watch=always`; plain `--watch` exits at once and the log says `pipeline watch "tailwind" exited (code 0)`. `examples/10-asset-pipeline.js` is the runnable version of all of this.

`markdown` is the option set handed to this instance's Remarkable — the renderer behind both `.md` partials and the `{{markdown}}` helper — so the two can never disagree. The three keys above are the ones kiss has a default for, **not** the ones it accepts: the block is passed through as-is, so any other Remarkable option (`typographer: true`, `langPrefix`) reaches the renderer without kiss knowing the name. `breaks: false` is deliberate and matches published v1: with `breaks: true` a paragraph hard-wrapped in the source renders one `<br />` per source line, breaking prose mid-sentence at whatever column the author happened to wrap at — set it to `true` only if your `.md` sources treat a newline as a real line break. Merged one level deep, like `sass`, `fetch` and `assets`, so `markdown: { breaks: true }` keeps `html` and `xhtmlOut` at their defaults. It applies per `Kiss` instance and is read in the constructor, **before** partials are registered: `.md` partials are rendered to HTML at registration, so setting it in config is the only way to reach them — mutating `kiss.remarkable` afterwards would change the helper but silently miss every partial (a later `kiss.registerPartials()` is what that would need).

`livereloadPort` lets two sites run side by side: give the second one its own value, or its pages would poll the first site's live reload server. A clash on the live reload port is logged and live reload is switched off for that site — the dev server keeps serving. A clash on `port` is fatal instead: nothing can be served without the HTTP server, so the bind failure is reported exactly once (`Dev server could not bind 127.0.0.1:3001 (EADDRINUSE): the site is not being served`), the watcher and live reload are closed so the process can exit, and `complete()` rejects with a `<dev server>` failure. The `Serving …` line is printed only once the server is actually listening. Use `port` (with its own `livereloadPort`) to run a second site. `devHost` binds the dev and live reload servers to loopback only; set it to `'0.0.0.0'` to open the preview to other devices on your network — live reload follows the host the page was loaded from, so a preview opened on a phone reloads from the machine serving it.

A key you pass explicitly as `undefined` takes its default (`port: process.env.PORT` with `PORT` unset gives 3001); `null` is a real value — it switches a folder off.

Setting `folders.src` re-derives `pages`, `assets`, `layouts`, `partials`, `models` and `controllers` from it (`${src}/${key}`), unless a given key is also set explicitly in the same `folders` object — `build` is independent and always defaults to `./public` regardless of `src`. Folder strings are normalised on the way in — a trailing slash or a backslash separator is tolerated (`'./src/assets/'` and `'.\\src\\assets'` both resolve to `'./src/assets'`).

## Helpers

Registered on `kiss.handlebars` for every instance; register your own on the same object.

- `markdown` — block (`{{#markdown}}...{{/markdown}}`) or string/model value (`{{markdown model.body}}`); rendered through `kiss.remarkable`, returned as safe HTML. `undefined` logs a warning and renders nothing; a `null`, plain object or array also renders nothing (with a warning), rather than throwing.
- `sass` — file path string (`{{{sass "src/assets/main.scss"}}}`) and/or an inline block (`{{#sass}}$c: red; body { color: $c; }{{/sass}}`); both may be combined. A relative file path resolves against **`process.cwd()`**, not `config.folders.assets` or the view's own location; an absolute path is used as given. `style` is `'expanded'` in `dev: true`, `'compressed'` otherwise; `loadPaths` comes from `config.sass.includePaths`.
- `offset(index)` — returns `index + 1`, for 1-based numbering: `{{offset @index}}` inside a `{{#each}}`.
- `stringify(obj)` — `JSON.stringify(obj, null, 3)`; `{{{stringify this}}}` to inspect what's in scope (triple braces — it's JSON, not HTML to escape).
- `lookup` — Handlebars' built-in `lookup`, plus a warning when the key is undefined: `lookup: 'moodleAccess' is undefined in handbooks/uob.hbs` (the view is named when the page context carries one, once per page per key). Return value and prototype-access safety are the built-in's, unchanged — a dynamic partial `{{> (lookup . 'key')}}` with a missing key still fails the build with `The partial undefined could not be found`; you now also get the key's name.
- `isActive` — block helper for nav active-state: `{{#isActive page href="/about"}}class="active"{{/isActive}}`. Hash keys: `href` (the link's path; an omitted or absent key is treated as `''`, not thrown on), `active` (default `'active'`, the string rendered as `{{active}}` inside the block when matched), `folderMatch` (default `false`). Both `href` and the page's own URL are reduced to the same key first — no leading/trailing slash, no file extension, no trailing `index` segment — so `href="/about"` matches the page whether it built to `about.html` or (`extensionLess: true`) `about/index.html`, and `/about`/`/about/` are always the same href. Exact key match by default; `folderMatch=true` also matches any page below `href` (`/blog` then matches `/blog/post-1`), and an empty `href` under `folderMatch` matches the home page only. A non-block usage, or a page context with no `pageURL`, logs a warning and renders the block as not-active rather than throwing.
- `canonical` — the current page's absolute URL: `{{canonical}}` → `https://example.com/about` for the page that built to `about.html`, `https://example.com/courses/` for the one that built to `courses/index.html`, and `https://example.com/` for the home page. **A directory index keeps a trailing slash** — that is the URL a static host (Netlify, GitHub Pages, nginx) serves, and it answers the bare `/courses` with a 301, so the slashed form is the one that returns 200. Under `extensionLess: true` every page but the home page builds to `<path>/<slug>/index.html` and so is a directory index too: its canonical is `https://example.com/about/`, again the URL the host serves without a redirect. Built from `config.siteUrl` and the page's own URL by the same code that writes `sitemap.xml`, so `<link rel="canonical" href="{{canonical}}">` and that page's `<loc>` are always the same string: extension dropped, a trailing `index` segment becoming the trailing slash, no double slash whether or not `siteUrl` ends in one. A page that overrides `siteUrl` for itself (`.page({ config: { siteUrl } })`) gets a canonical URL on that domain. It takes no arguments; `{{canonical this}}`, the shape a hand-rolled v1 helper usually had, works too. With no `siteUrl` it renders nothing and logs one warning per page; so does a render with no page context.
- `absUrl` — `config.siteUrl` joined to any site-relative path: `{{absUrl "/img/card.png"}}` → `https://example.com/img/card.png` (for `og:image`, an RSS link, a feed). `/about` and `about` are both `https://example.com/about`; a trailing slash is preserved, not trimmed (`about/` → `https://example.com/about/`), and a trailing `index` segment becomes one (`/courses/index.html` → `https://example.com/courses/`); a file extension is kept (`css/site.css` stays `css/site.css`, unlike `canonical`'s page URL); a path that already has a scheme (`https://cdn.example/x.png`) is returned untouched, `siteUrl` or not; `{{absUrl}}` with no path is `{{canonical}}`. A non-string path logs a warning and renders nothing.
- `asset` — the path of a file `.copyAssets()` put in the build, under whatever cache-busting policy `config.assets` sets: `{{asset "css/site.css"}}` renders `css/site.css` with no policy, `css/site.a1b2c3d4.css` under `assets: { hash: true }`, and `css/site.css?v=1.4.5` under `assets: { version: '1.4.5' }`. The template says which file it wants; the config says how it is cached, so changing the policy never touches a template. Ask for the path the file has when nothing is renaming it — a `.scss` source by its compiled `.css` name (`css/site.css`, not `css/site.scss`) — with or without a leading slash. It renders **no leading slash**, so the template picks the base: `href="/{{asset "css/site.css"}}"` for a root-relative link, `href="{{root}}{{asset "css/site.css"}}"` for one that also works opened off the file system, and `{{absUrl (asset "css/site.css")}}` for an absolute URL (the query string and the hashed extension both survive). A URL that already has a scheme is passed through untouched. A path that is not in the build renders as you wrote it and logs one warning per page naming it, rather than failing the page; a non-string path logs a warning and renders nothing.
- `link` — the URL of a page **by its identity**, so a template never guesses one: `<a href="{{link "about"}}">` renders `/about.html`, or `/about/` on an `extensionLess` site, and `{{link "blog/post" slug=post.slug}}` renders that post's path. Every page has an `id` — by default its view's route without the extension (`blog/listing.hbs` → `blog/listing`), and for a `.pages()` item the registration's route (or its `id`) plus the item's slug (`blog/post/the-cascara-experiment`) — and `id:` on the page options (or on a fan-out **record**) sets it yourself. What it renders is the path the host actually serves: `/`, `/about.html`, `/courses/`, `/blog/the-cascara-experiment/`, `/data/index.json`. It is **root-relative**: for a site served from a path prefix, or a link that has to be absolute (an `og:url`, a feed), use `{{link "about" absolute=true}}` → `https://example.com/about.html`; for the pretty form the sitemap and `{{canonical}}` emit, `{{link "about" canonical=true}}` → `/about` (wrap it in `{{absUrl}}` to make that absolute). **It is the one helper that fails the build**: an id no page claims, an id two pages' *defaults* both arrived at (neither keeps it — a `notice` names the views and asks you to set one), or a page with `generate: false` (which claims no id) fails the page that linked it, naming the id and the view that asked — a link is a promise, and unlike a hand-written path it is checkable at render. Under `dev: true` it warns and renders `#` instead, so the live preview shows you both the page and the mistake. Two pages claiming the same **explicit** id fail the build outright, like two pages claiming one output path.
- `env` — block helper gated on `config.dev`: `{{#env is="dev"}}dev-only{{else}}prod-only{{/env}}`. Hash key: `is` (required string, case-insensitive substring match — `"dev"`/`"prod"`). A missing or non-string `is` logs an error and renders neither branch.

## Writing llms.txt

`llms.txt` is the curated, AI-facing index of a site — what an answer engine reads before it crawls. `.llms()` builds one from the pages already registered, so it cannot list a URL the site does not serve or a title the page does not carry. End to end:

```js
kiss
  .page({ view: 'index.hbs', title: 'A1K9 Training', description: 'Dog training and behaviour work in South Wales' })
  .pages({ view: 'courses/course.hbs', model: 'courses', path: 'courses' })
  .page({ view: 'rota.hbs', ignoreLlms: true }) // in the sitemap, out of the index
  .generate()
  .sitemap()
  .llms({
    title: 'A1K9 Training',
    // Inline text, or a path to a file: `summary: 'src/content/summary.md'`
    summary: 'Dog behaviour and obedience training in South Wales, run by Gaynor Probert.',
    sections: { root: 'Pages', courses: 'Courses' },
    notes: 'src/content/llms-notes.md',
  })
```

writes:

```markdown
# A1K9 Training

> Dog behaviour and obedience training in South Wales, run by Gaynor Probert.

## Pages

- [A1K9 Training](https://a1k9training.co.uk/): Dog training and behaviour work in South Wales

## Courses

- [Bronze obedience](https://a1k9training.co.uk/courses/bronze-obedience): Six weeks, group class
```

## Checking a build

`npx kiss-ssg check <script> [args…]` runs a site's own build script as a dry run: the build is staged and then discarded, so the build folder is neither emptied nor written, and what you get back is the verdict instead of the output. (`npx kiss-ssg aikb <script>` is the same run with one thing added — see **Recording the knowledge base** below. Both take `--summary`, `--against <file>` and `--help`.) Arguments after the script are passed through to it, so a site that takes a season or a cohort is checked the way it is run. It prints a JSON array with one report per `Kiss` instance the script created — a script that builds several outputs gets several reports:

```json
[
  {
    "ok": false,
    "mode": "check",
    "buildDir": "./public",
    "duration": 160,
    "pages": [
      {
        "view": "index.hbs",
        "buildTo": "./public/index.html",
        "ok": true,
        "hash": "9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31"
      }
    ],
    "failures": [
      {
        "view": "stockists/stockist.hbs [item 3: harbour-market-stall]",
        "buildTo": null,
        "message": "Incomplete stockist record — missing address"
      }
    ],
    "assets": [{ "source": "css/site.css", "target": "css/site.605b52d7.css" }],
    "sitemap": "./public/sitemap.xml",
    "pipeline": [{ "name": "tailwind", "ok": true, "duration": 420 }],
    "llms": "./public/llms.txt",
    "aikb": {
      "folder": "AIKB",
      "written": false,
      "notes": {
        "missing": ["AIKB/notes/controllers/stockist.md"],
        "dead": ["AIKB/notes/pipeline/postcss.md"],
        "stale": ["AIKB/notes/pipeline/tailwind.md"],
        "dangling": ["AIKB/notes/pipeline/tailwind.md: src/assets/old.css"]
      },
      "subjects": [
        {
          "kind": "controllers",
          "id": "stockist.js",
          "note": "notes/controllers/stockist.md",
          "hash": "9f2a1c4e8b70d3a6c5e1f08b2d47a93c6e5b1d20"
        },
        {
          "kind": "pipeline",
          "id": "tailwind",
          "note": "notes/pipeline/tailwind.md",
          "hash": "3c81be07f4a2d95e6b0c7f13a8d24e59b6710fc8"
        }
      ]
    },
    "links": {
      "checked": 24,
      "broken": [{ "page": "./public/about.html", "href": "/news/gone" }]
    },
    "redirects": {
      "file": "./public/_redirects",
      "aliases": 2,
      "removed": ["/news/autumn-2025.html"],
      "collisions": [],
      "moved": [
        { "id": "blog/post", "from": "/blog/old-slug/", "to": "/blog/new-slug/" }
      ]
    },
    "feed": "./public/feed.xml"
  }
]
```

**Exit code 1** if any report is `ok: false`, if the script itself exited non-zero, or if no report was written at all — a script that never awaits `complete()` reports nothing, which is itself the finding. Exit 0 with `ok: true` on every report is the only passing result. The site's own build log goes to stderr, so stdout is nothing but the JSON. `--summary` prints one line per site instead (`ok ./public (check) — 6 pages, 0 failed, 2 assets, 153ms`, plus a line per failure, then — for a site with a knowledge base — the four note findings, one line each: `  note missing: <path>` per subject nobody has explained, `  note dead: <path>` per note whose subject is gone, `  note stale: <path>` per note whose stamp is no longer its subject's hash, and `  note dangling: <path>: <token>` per file reference in a note that resolves to nothing — and then `  broken link: <page> -> <href>` per internal reference that resolves to nothing, `  removed without redirect: <path>` per page the last record wrote that this build does not and no alias covers, `  moved without redirect: <from> -> <to> (<id>)` per page the record and this build share an `id` with whose path changed and whose old path no alias covers, and `  alias collides with a page: <path>` per alias a live page already answers — the two rename findings name **served URLs** (`/courses/`, `/about.html`, `/`), the addresses a reader's links carry, never the `index.html` files behind them; none of them changes the exit code); it is read wherever you write it, and a site that needs the word `--summary` itself takes it after a bare `--`. `--against <file>` (before the script, and it takes the next word as its file) names the baseline for the diff described below; a site that has recorded a knowledge base is diffed against it **without** the flag.

**`check` diffs this build against an earlier one.** With no flag, the baseline is the site's own `<config.folders.aikb>/last-build.json` when that file exists — the state of the site when its knowledge base was last recorded, so the answer is "what has changed since that piece of work closed" rather than "since somebody last ran a build". `--against <file>` names a different baseline and always wins. The file is a report somebody kept: a `KISS_REPORT` JSON Lines file, the JSON array `check` itself prints, or a single report object — all three are read, so you do not have to say which you have. Reports are paired by `buildDir` (a script that builds several sites gets several diffs), pages are matched by output path and compared by `hash`, so the answer is about the bytes a browser would receive rather than about which files were touched. A page whose `hash` is `null` on either side counts as changed, never as unchanged. Under `--summary` the diff prints under that site's line:

```
ok ./public (check) — 6 pages, 0 failed, 2 assets, 153ms
  + ./public/news/spring-2026.html
  - ./public/news/autumn-2025.html
  ~ ./public/news/index.html
  = 3 unchanged
```

Without `--summary` stdout becomes `{ "reports": [...], "diff": [...] }` instead of the bare array whenever there is a diff to print — under `--against`, or under `check` with a recorded baseline — and `diff` is in the same order as `reports`, one entry each: `{ buildDir, added, removed, changed, unchanged }`, the three lists holding output paths, sorted. A missing or unreadable file is a usage error (exit 1, nothing built). The diff never changes the exit code: it describes the build, it does not judge it.

**Driving it without the bin** (a CI step, a harness of your own): `KISS_CHECK=1` turns any build into a check — `cleanBuild` becomes `'atomic'`, `dev` becomes `false`, and the staging folder is discarded when `complete()` settles whether the build passed or failed, so nothing published is touched. Any value counts as set except `0`, `false` and the empty string. `KISS_REPORT=<file>` appends each settled build's report to `<file>` as JSON Lines, one line per `Kiss` instance. `KISS_AIKB=1` (same rule again) is what `kiss-ssg aikb` adds on top of those two. None of the three changes the script's own exit code — that is the caller's decision, and the bin's.

One thing a check deliberately does do: it runs `config.assets.pipeline` exactly as a build does, so it is not read-only over your working tree — the steps regenerate whatever they generate, into your source, which is why there is nothing extra for the check to discard.

**Broken internal links.** Every settled non-dev build scans its own output and reports what it found as `report().links` — `{ checked, broken: [{ page, href }] }`, and one `  broken link: <page> -> <href>` line per finding under `--summary`. **Checked:** the `href`, `src`, each `srcset` candidate and `action` of every `a`, `link`, `script`, `img`, `source`, `video`, `audio`, `iframe` and `form` the page wrote — resolved root-relative against the build folder and relative against the page's own directory, accepting a file that is there, a page this build wrote, `<path>/` → `<path>/index.html`, an extension-less `<path>` → `<path>.html` or `<path>/index.html`, and an asset under the name `{{asset}}` actually emitted. An absolute URL on your own `siteUrl` is **internal** — that is what catches a renamed slug still linked from a nav or a `{{canonical}}`. **Ignored:** another origin, a protocol-relative `//host/x`, `mailto:`, `tel:`, `data:`, `javascript:`, a bare `#fragment` and an empty value; a query string and a fragment are stripped before resolving. **`{{link}}` and the checker are two halves of one thing:** the helper renders a path the resolver accepts by construction — a file, a `<path>/` directory index, or `/` — so a site whose internal hrefs are all `{{link}}` reports `broken: []`, and the scan stays the net for the hand-written references beside them. One qualifier: the pages the scan knows about are the ones that **wrote bytes**, so a `{{link}}` to a page that failed to render *is* reported broken on every page that linked it — which is the honest answer, since no such file was published. Under `assets.hash` a hardcoded `/css/site.css` **is** a finding: the file on disk is `css/site.<hash>.css`, so use `{{asset}}`. The finding is advisory — it never changes `ok` and never changes the exit code. `links: { check: false }` turns the scan off, and a **dev build or a watch rebuild always reports `links: null`**: a scoped re-render has not rewritten every page, so there is nothing honest to scan.

**Redirects, and what a rename left behind.** A page's `aliases` are the old URL paths it now answers, and every settled build writes them into `<build>/_redirects` — the Netlify and Cloudflare Pages format, one `/<old> <new> 301` per line, sorted and byte-stable, where `<new>` is the page's canonical path (`/`, `/courses/`, `/about`), the same string its `{{canonical}}` and its `<loc>` in `sitemap.xml` carry. No other format, and no meta-refresh. A site with no aliases writes **no file at all**, so a hand-written `_redirects` you keep in `src/assets/` is copied into the build and left alone. `report().redirects` is `{ file, aliases, removed, collisions, moved }`, or `null` when there is nothing to say — no alias anywhere in the site, no removal and no move, which is the ordinary answer for a site that uses neither feature and for a recorded site nothing has happened to. Three advisory findings ride with it. `removed` names the pages the **last record** (`<config.folders.aikb>/last-build.json`, written by `npx kiss-ssg aikb`) wrote that this build does not, minus any an alias now covers — a page that vanished with no redirect. Both rename findings name the page's **served URL** — `/courses/` for a directory index, `/about.html` for a file page, `/` for the home page — because that is what a reader's link says and what an `aliases` entry has to match; the comparison behind them is made on the output files. It is the one finding that needs a record: without one it is empty, and an unreadable one is treated the same way. Paths on both sides are compared build-relative, so a record made from one working directory and a check run from another still agree. `moved` names the pages the last record and this build both have — paired by the page's `id`, not by its path — whose output path changed and whose old path no alias covers: `{ id, from, to }` per page as served URLs, sorted by `from`, and one `notice` each carrying the fix (`add "<from>" to that page's aliases`). It needs a record too, and it needs an id on **both** sides: a page whose identity is stable is one this finding can follow across a rename, and a page whose identity changed with it is not. That is a real limit — a `.pages()` item's default id embeds its slug (`blog/post/<slug>`), so renaming a post's slug changes its id as well as its path and the event is reported as a `removed` instead. `moved` is for pages with a stable id: a `.page()` page whose `path`, `slug` or `ext` moved, and any page (a fan-out record included) that carries an explicit `id`. A move suppresses the matching `removed`, so one rename is one finding. `collisions` names the aliases a live page already answers — its canonical path (`/about`) or the file itself (`/about.html`) — because on both hosts a non-forced rule at a source a real file occupies is **silently ignored**, doing nothing at all; an alias two pages both claim is listed for the same reason. Neither moves `ok` or the exit code.

Two things a check cannot make true. A site that **reads its own build folder back** after `complete()` (an index that lists the version folders on disk) sees a folder nothing was published into, so it reports fewer of them than a real build would. And a site with `cleanBuild: false` that relies on files an **earlier** build left behind starts from an empty staging folder, since check mode stages everything.

### Recording the knowledge base

`npx kiss-ssg aikb <script> [args…]` writes the site's own knowledge base into `config.folders.aikb` (default `./AIKB`): a map of the site as the build saw it, for the developer who comes back to it in two years. It runs exactly the build `check` runs — staged and discarded, publishing nothing — and the folder is the only thing it leaves behind. Nothing else writes it: there is no API call, and an ordinary build, a `check`, a dev build and a watch rebuild all write none of it. Recording is a **ceremony**: run it when a piece of work is finished, and commit the folder. That is what makes the diff above mean "since this work opened" instead of "since the last time anybody built".

**It refuses to record a build that did not work.** A failed build writes nothing and the summary says `  not recorded — build failed`; the exit code is `check`'s. A dev build (`dev: true`) writes nothing either. The previous record stays exactly as it was — a knowledge base that describes a broken build is worse than a slightly old one.

**Four files, all byte-stable across two identical records** — nothing is timestamped and every list is sorted, so recording an unchanged site twice leaves `git status` clean and any diff in the folder is a real change to the shape of the site:

| File              | Written                      | What it holds                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `README.md`       | once, if absent; never again | what the folder is, which files are generated, how to write and stamp a note, what the four findings mean, and what `site.md` is for                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `site-map.md`     | every record                 | the map as markdown: the site's URL, build folder and source folders; a row per page (output path, the page's `id`, view, model source, controller source, the partials and layouts it actually rendered); the partial → pages index; models and controllers with the pages that used them; the asset pipeline's steps; and a `## Subjects` table (kind, subject, its note, the first 12 characters of its hash) |
| `site-map.json`   | every record                 | the same map as data, including `subjects` with each subject's whole hash — what a note's `subject-hash` stamp is copied from                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `last-build.json` | every record                 | that build's report with every timing dropped — the baseline `check` diffs against                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

The folder is **source, meant to be committed**: it sits outside `config.folders.build`, survives `cleanBuild`, and is not created at all until you record one. Setting `folders.aikb: null` switches it off entirely.

**Having the folder is not the same as opting in.** A build reports `report().aikb` when `folders.aikb` is set *and* `<folder>/site-map.json` is there — the one file only a record writes. Until then `aikb` is `null` and nothing is built: the default `./AIKB` is harmless in a repository whose `AIKB/` is something else (hand-written module notes, say). Once a site has recorded, every build — including a `check` — reports the folder and the note findings, with `written: false`.

**Notes are yours; the engine never writes one.** A map says what the site is; a note says why, which no build can work out. Three kinds of subject carry judgement and each wants a note under `AIKB/notes/`, at a path derived mechanically from its id: a controller **file** (`stockist.js` → `notes/controllers/stockist.md`), a model fetched by **URL** (`https://api.example.com/v2/events?x=1` → `notes/models/api.example.com-v2-events.md`, host and path, query dropped) and an **asset pipeline step** (`tailwind` → `notes/pipeline/tailwind.md`). Plain pages, partials and `.json` models are deliberately not subjects — a note saying "renders the about page" is noise. An inline controller or an object model has no file to attach a note to and is not a subject either.

**Every subject carries a hash, and a note may be stamped with it.** `site-map.json`'s `subjects` is `{ kind, id, note, hash }` per subject, sorted, and `site-map.md` has the same as a `## Subjects` table (the hash shortened to 12 characters): sha1 of the controller file's bytes, or of the pipeline step's `run` string, and `null` for a URL model — whose id *is* the subject, so there is nothing for a hash to add. Copy that hash into the note's frontmatter as `subject-hash: <sha1>` when you write or review the note:

```markdown
---
subject-hash: 9f2a1c4e8b70d3a6c5e1f08b2d47a93c6e5b1d20
---

## What it does
```

The engine never writes a stamp, and an unstamped note is never reported stale — stamping is opt-in, per note. The hash to stamp with is on **every** build's report as `report().aikb.subjects`, not only on a record's: at the moment a stale note is found, `site-map.json` on disk still describes the previous record, so the report is the only place the current hash exists.

**Four findings, on `report().aikb.notes`, every build.** **missing** — a subject with no note. **dead** — a note under `notes/` whose subject is not in the map. **stale** — a note whose `subject-hash` stamp is not its subject's current hash (a URL model can never be stale). **dangling** — `"<note path>: <token>"` for a backticked token in a note that looks like a file reference and resolves to nothing: not a file on disk, not a page view or output path, not a partial name, a model or controller name, a folder in the map, or a path under the AIKB folder. The dangling filter is deliberately narrow — a token needs a `/` or a known extension, and must hold no spaces, `<`, `>`, `*`, `{`, `}` or `$`; fenced code blocks, trailing-slash folders and anything with a URI scheme are skipped — because a lint that fires on every note is one people learn to ignore. None of the four is a build failure and none changes an exit code.

**`AIKB/site.md` is the page about the whole site**, rather than about any one subject: authored, evergreen, and never written by the engine. It is scanned for `dangling` references when it is there, and checked for nothing else. The generated `AIKB/README.md` names its five sections — What this site is and who for · How it is deployed · Conventions · Standing gotchas · Retired feedback — and the `kiss-memory-consolidate` skill is what maintains it.

A recorded folder to read: [examples/9-migrated-from-v1/AIKB/](examples/9-migrated-from-v1/AIKB/) — recorded with `cd examples && npx kiss-ssg aikb 9-migrated-from-v1.js`, with one authored note beside the map.

## Docs

- [README.md](README.md): full usage docs, worked examples for `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.sitemap()`, the helpers list.
- [examples/](examples/): ships in the package, so an agent working in a consuming project can read `node_modules/kiss-ssg/examples/README.md` and run a copy from there. Two tiers. Examples 1–6 and 10 are the feature reference, one idea each — scan, page/model/controller, `.pages()` fan-out, layouts and partials, helpers, sitemap and llms.txt, and an external tool in `config.assets.pipeline`. Examples 7–9 and 11 are exemplars, whole sites to copy by shape rather than a single feature: 7 is versioned outputs, one build per season; 8 is a site built from a folder of records with one broken one, fed and validated in the controller; 9 is every v1 → v2 migration recipe as running code, in a site that builds clean, and it ships the recorded `AIKB/` folder (see **Recording the knowledge base**); 11 is a blog — posts as a folder fan-out with a controller file, a paginated listing at `/blog/` and `/blog/page/2/`, tag pages as a second fan-out over a computed array, `.feed({ section: 'blog' })`, one renamed post whose record carries `aliases` so `_redirects` is written, and a recorded `AIKB/` with two authored notes. Every example builds and exits by default (`node examples/<N>-name.js`, or `npm run eg<N>`); pass `--dev` to run examples 1–6, 8, 9, 10 and 11 as a live dev server instead (7 takes a season slug in place of `--dev`). Example 8 is the only one that exits non-zero, and it does so on purpose; example 11 takes `--broken`, which adds one bad link so a `check` reports exactly one `broken link:` finding.
- [types/](types/): TypeScript declarations, generated from the JSDoc in `lib/` and shipped in the package (`package.json`'s `types`, and an `exports` map whose `.` entry resolves `types` → `./types/kiss.d.ts` and both `import` and `require` → `./lib/kiss.js`). A plain-JavaScript site gets full completion and checking by putting `// @ts-check` at the top of its build script — no TypeScript, no `@types/` package. Every option type is reachable from the one entry: `/** @type {import('kiss-ssg').KissConfigInput} */` on the config object, `import('kiss-ssg').PageOptions` / `PagesOptions` on page options, `import('kiss-ssg').KissController` on a controller, and `import('kiss-ssg').BuildError` to cast the error `complete()` rejects with before reading `err.failures`. Also exported: `KissConfig` (the resolved config a view sees), `KissFolders`, `PageOptionsPatch` (what a controller returns), `BuildData`, `BuildFailure`, `BuildReport` (what `report()` returns) with `BuildPage`, `BuildAsset` and `BuildReportFailure`, `SitemapOptions`, `SitemapUrl`, `LlmsOptions`, `WatchOptions`. Arbitrary keys are allowed on the config and on page options — they reach the template — so only the documented keys are checked; `folders` is closed, so a misspelled folder name is an error.
- [plugins/kiss-ssg/](plugins/kiss-ssg/): a Claude Code plugin, installed with `/plugin marketplace add cprobert/kiss-ssg` then `/plugin install kiss-ssg@kiss-ssg`. Four skills, each named `kiss-<something>` for easy discovery — `kiss-site-new`, `kiss-page-add`, `kiss-site-migrate`, `kiss-build-check` — which sequence this file and the examples rather than restating them, and whose descriptions are written so Claude reaches for them on its own without being invoked by name. The plugin does not ship in the npm tarball, only in the repository; a project's CLAUDE.md can import this file directly with `@node_modules/kiss-ssg/llms.txt`.
- [plugins/kiss-memory/](plugins/kiss-memory/): the sibling plugin from the same marketplace (`/plugin install kiss-memory@kiss-ssg`). Five skills: `kiss-site-brief` (the returning-developer briefing over the recorded `AIKB/`, every statement labelled generated or recollection), `kiss-branch-open`, `kiss-branch-pulse` and `kiss-branch-close` (a piece of work on a site, verified against the `check` diff, with the close the only moment `kiss-ssg aikb` records), and `kiss-memory-consolidate` (folds session logs into `AIKB/site.md` and repairs the notes `check` reports as stale, dangling or dead).
- [lib/](lib/): the engine — `kiss.js` (orchestrator, public API), `kiss-page.js` (one page's render), and one module per concern (`config`, `logger`, `handlebars-helpers`, `partials`, `dependency-graph`, `assets`, `asset-manifest`, `sass`, `model-resolver`, `fetch-policy`, `controller-resolver`, `sitemap`, `dev-server`, `watcher`, `utils`, `build-report`, `check`, `pipeline`, `llms`, `aikb`). Per-module notes: [AIKB/](AIKB/).

## Migrating from v1

- **Node ≥22.12.0 first** (`package.json` `engines.node`) — check this before anything else: v2 will not install or run below it. If your project pins a dev Node version the way this repo's own `.nvmrc` does, bump yours before touching any code.
- ESM-only (`import Kiss from 'kiss-ssg'`); CJS `require()` still works on Node ≥22.12.
- `folders.root` and `folders.static` are gone — no module ever read them, so a config passing them gets nothing rather than a quiet no-op; delete the keys. The six keys v2 derives from `folders.src`/`folders.build` unless overridden (`pages`, `assets`, `layouts`, `partials`, `models`, `controllers`) are documented in `## Config` above.
- The `generate` callback now fires after files are written, not before.
- v1 logged a page's render/write failure and resolved anyway; v2's `complete()` rejects with an `AggregateError` listing the failed views (`err.failures` = `[{ view, buildTo, error }]`). The v1 callback-style idiom — `kiss.generate(function () { this.complete(function () { ... }) })` — now leaves that rejection unhandled the first time a page fails, so give `complete()` a `.catch`:
  ```js
  kiss
    .scan()
    .generate()
    .complete()
    .catch((err) => {
      for (const f of err.failures) {
        console.error(`${f.view} | ${f.buildTo} | ${f.error.message}`)
      }
      process.exitCode = 1
    })
  ```
  A failed build never runs `complete()`'s own callback, so anything you did there — writing a sitemap, generating an index, kicking off a deploy — has to run again in the `catch`. And a chain that ends at `.generate()` with no `.complete()` never sees any of this: it keeps exiting 0 on a broken build, so every deploy script must `await complete()` (or otherwise attach a rejection handler to it) to catch a failure.
- Handlebars is per-instance — register helpers on `kiss.handlebars`, not the global `handlebars` module. Partials are registered there too, so a helper reading the global `handlebars.partials` renders nothing; use `kiss.handlebars.partials` or the native dynamic partial `{{> (lookup this "name")}}`. Every entry of `kiss.handlebars.partials` is a function — a compiled template that also records which page invoked it — so a helper that renders an entry by name must accept a function; the one-line form is under `.registerPartials()` above.
- `utils` is a named export (`import { utils } from 'kiss-ssg'`), not `kiss-ssg/libs/utils.js`. The `exports` map has one entry, so any deep path into the package (`kiss-ssg/lib/…`, `kiss-ssg/libs/…`) now fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` instead of half-working — everything public is reachable from `'kiss-ssg'` itself.
- Controllers may `export default` instead of `module.exports =`.
- Duplicate output paths, including `.pages()` fan-out where a controller yields the same slug twice, are no longer written twice: the second page is not built and the collision is a build failure, so `complete()` rejects naming the path (`Page already processed: <path>`) — v1 wrote whichever page came last. If you relied on that v1 skip to give one source priority over another — a low-priority fan-out registered last, on the assumption the engine would silently drop whatever slug a higher-priority source had already claimed — dedupe the slugs yourself before registering instead:
  ```js
  const claimed = new Set(catalogItems.map((c) => c.slug))
  const rdItems = allRdItems.filter((r) => !claimed.has(r.slug))
  kiss.pages({ view: 'rd.hbs', model: rdItems /* ... */ })
  ```
- **Unchanged in v2**, so there is nothing to migrate here even though it looks load-bearing: the per-page `generate: false` option (default `true`) still skips building one page; `callback.call(this, ...)` still binds the `Kiss` instance inside `generate`/`complete`/`sitemap` callbacks; the per-page `ext` option; `copyAssets(sourceDir, targetDir)` to a second directory; `viewStats()`/`getModelByID()`. `_stack` (and any other underscore-prefixed field) is internal and unversioned — code reading `_stack[].buildTo`/`_stack[].page.options` works today by accident; `.sitemap()` is the supported way to enumerate registered pages.
